source_artifacts.locator: approval queue (as shown to the analyst)

capabilities.target: A user's MFA methods and temporary pass issuance

inputs.source: Support ticket, including tickets emailed in by contractors and vendors

instructions.note: The rule 'send the temporary access pass to the person who opened the ticket' assumes the ticket opener is the account owner, with no structural check. Runtime notes explicitly confirm this is not the case: 'The temporary pass goes to whoever opened the ticket, not to the account owner.'

elements.name: External ticket submitters (including contractors/vendors emailing in)
Temporary access pass delivery to ticket requester

controls.name: Service desk analyst approval in the queue tool before any reset runs
controls.decay_rationale: Raw-action review does not decay with model capability, but high volume (about 400 approvals/shift across two analysts, 'most are routine') produces approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403), and the gate gives the analyst no way to verify that the ticket's self-reported requester is the target account's owner, so it narrows but does not sever the identity-confusion path. Fails if the approval requirement is removed or if autonomy increases beyond it.

controls.name: Recipient identity verification bound to the account's system-of-record contact
controls.decay_rationale: Would be enforced outside the model against a system-of-record contact (not the ticket's self-reported requester field), making the pass-delivery sink unreachable for requester-impersonation attempts regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Tamper-evident audit log binding reset and pass-delivery actions to analyst, ticket, and verified recipient
controls.decay_rationale: Detective logging enforced at the IdP/chat integration layer, independent of model behavior; does not prevent misuse but restores attributability.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): ticket-controlled target and requester let any external sender obtain another user's MFA reset pass

attack_path.note: External email, including contractor-submitted tickets, supplies free text naming the target account; the sender address becomes the 'requester' used downstream.
Agent looks up the user named in the ticket to resolve the target account.
Agent resets the named user's MFA after analyst approval; the queue shows target, requester, and ticket text but has no way to confirm the requester is the account owner.
Agent sends the resulting temporary access pass to 'whoever opened the ticket' (the untrusted email sender), not the verified account owner.

forecast.watch_signal: Autonomy raised beyond A2 for cap.mfa_reset/cap.send_temp_pass (approval no longer required), or the approval-gate requirement disabled or bypassed in the queue tool or orchestration config.

evidence.observation: States: 'The temporary pass goes to whoever opened the ticket, not to the account owner.'
States: 'Contractors and vendors can email tickets in. The requester field is the email sender.'
Instructs the agent to look up the user named in the ticket, reset their MFA, and send the temporary access pass to the person who opened the ticket.
Shows Target, Requested by, and full ticket text to the analyst, but provides no field or step to confirm the requester is the target account's owner.
States two analysts approve about 400 requests per shift and 'most are routine', indicating approval volume consistent with approval fatigue.

recommendations.action: Verify the temp-pass recipient against the target account's system-of-record contact (e.g., a pre-registered phone number or manager-confirmed channel) before cap.send_temp_pass executes, instead of defaulting to whoever opened the ticket.

Surface an explicit target-vs-requester identity match check in the approval queue, flagging or blocking resets where the ticket's claimed requester does not correspond to the target account owner, especially for externally submitted tickets.
Add secondary review or reduce per-analyst throughput for resets originating from external or contractor email addresses to counter approval fatigue at roughly 400 requests per shift.

findings.title: No attributable, tamper-evident record binding MFA resets and temp-pass deliveries to a verified recipient (repudiation gap)

forecast.watch_signal: Autonomy increased so resets or pass deliveries occur with even less human involvement, with still no independent attributable record of who approved what for whom.

evidence.observation: No logging system, audit trail, or tamper-evident record is described anywhere in the provided artifacts beyond the approval queue's on-screen display.

recommendations.action: Implement a tamper-evident log that binds each MFA reset and temp-pass delivery to the approving analyst, the ticket id, the target account, and the actual delivery destination used.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent authenticates to the IdP and queue tool with its own service identity; ticket content cannot spoof the agent process itself.
No capability lets ticket content modify the agent's own prompt, tool definitions, or configuration; there is no configure-self capability.
Disclosure of the temporary pass occurs through the send_temp_pass egress flow, covered separately as el.temp_pass_flow.
Artifacts do not state step limits, per-ticket runtime bounds, or safeguards against runaway or looping agent behavior.
Artifacts do not describe whether originating email headers or sender identity are retained to attribute a ticket to a specific external submitter later.
The inbound ticket flow carries the submitter's own text into the agent; it does not itself expose internal data outward.
Artifacts do not state whether a single sender is rate-limited in how many tickets can be submitted, which bears on queue flooding.
The temp pass is generated by the IdP and passed via an internal tool call to the chat system; no described mechanism lets an outsider alter it in transit.
Sending one temporary-pass message per ticket is not itself a resource-exhaustion vector.
Analysts authenticate to the queue tool directly through its own login; ticket content cannot spoof an analyst's identity.
No mechanism is described by which ticket content could alter an approval record after an analyst has acted on it.
The queue displays ticket data only to authorized analysts inside the trust boundary; no external disclosure path is described.
Artifacts describe steady-state volume of about 400 requests per shift but do not state whether the queue can be deliberately flooded to outage.
The queue only approves or rejects a proposed action; it has no independent mechanism to grant access beyond what is requested.
The agent calls the IdP with its own service credential; ticket content has no described path to spoof that service identity.
No mechanism is described for ticket content to alter IdP configuration or stored directory records directly.
idp.read_user results are used internally to resolve the ticket; their external disclosure is covered under el.temp_pass_flow.
Artifacts do not state whether idp.reset_mfa calls are rate-limited at the identity provider layer.
Artifacts do not state whether the requester's claimed identity is cryptographically verified or only a self-asserted email address.

rating.rationale: An untrusted source (support tickets, including ones emailed in by external contractors and vendors) directly determines both which account's MFA is reset (a credential-access, partially-reversible S3 action) and who receives the resulting temporary access pass (an S3 egress of a live credential), because the design sends the pass to 'whoever opened the ticket' rather than to a verified account owner, as runtime notes explicitly confirm. The only control, a human analyst approval gate, reviews raw ticket data (target, requester, full text) but has no field or step to confirm the requester is the account owner, and runs at high volume (about 400 approvals/shift across two analysts, 'most are routine'), producing approval fatigue that further erodes it. Inherent risk is critical (untrusted source reaching an S3 credential-issuance sink in one chain); the raw-action gate's single tier of credit at high volume brings residual to high, short of severing the path. If the approval requirement is loosened (autonomy_increase) or disabled (control_removal), the one existing control disappears entirely and risk returns to critical, which the forecast reflects. A secondary property finding notes the design describes no tamper-evident record binding resets and pass deliveries to a verified recipient, independently capped at high per rubric section 5a.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts (system prompt, approval-queue mockup, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP/tool manifest, IdP API scope documentation, or logging/audit configuration was provided; the credential breadth of idp.reset_mfa and the existence of any audit trail are inferred from narrative descriptions, which lowers confidence on finding f2.

Whether the approval queue retains records tied to the approving analyst's identity, and whether email sender addresses are authenticated corporate accounts versus open contractor inboxes, is not described in the artifacts.
